> **Note:**The FAA calls this a remote pilot certificate rather than a license. Worth knowing when you go through their site.

> **Note:** For those planning to do research with Dr. Macfarlane, iff you have questions, contact me at `cojow@icloud.com`. 

## Before You Start

### Eligibility

Information about the exam itself can be found [here](https://www.faa.gov/uas/commercial_operators/become_a_drone_pilot).
It also walks through the preperation and what to do after the test. 
That is the definitive source, and trumps any information found here.

The general requirements are as follows:

- Be at least 16 years old
- Be able to read, speak, write, and understand English
- Be in a physical and mental condition to safely fly a drone
- Pass the initial aeronautical knowledge exam: "Unmanned Aircraft General – Small (UAG)"

### TRUST Recreational Drone Certification

Start with obtaining your TRUST Recreational Drone Certification.
The FAA lists all of the approved (and free) test administrators [here](https://www.faa.gov/uas/recreational_flyers/knowledge_test_updates).
I used Pilot Institute, but any of them work.

It is not required to obtain your Part 107, but is useful as a first overview of drone regulation.
You'll create an account and go through ~20 minutes of training explaining what you can and can't do as a recreational flyer.
There are four quizzes you take as you review the material, and at the end you receive a pdf of your certificate (They delete your account after you download the certificate, so make sure you save it somewhere safe.)

## Creating a FAA Account

This will give you a FAA tracking number (FTN), which will be needed to register for your exam and certificate.
Do this before you try to schedule anything, since you can't register for the test without it.

1. Go to the [iacra website](https://iacra.faa.gov/IACRA/SelectRoles.aspx).
2. Select Applicant, scroll down and click "agree to TOS and continue".
3. Fill out the User Profile Information. Skip the section that says Airman certificate number.
    Enter personal info, security questions, and create a username and password.
4. You will have to set up an authenticator app, either here or when registering for the exam.

## Studying

There is a lot out there for test prep. This section is a mix of what I did and the resources from the CE Drone Measurements Class being piloted at BYU.

- Study for the test intensely several days before you take the test.
    There is so much that you need to know only for the test that cramming is what I recommend.
    Plan a day for the test, set aside several hours each day beforehand for studying, and then schedule the test.
- I watched ["FREE Part 107 Study Guide - FAA Drone Certification Exam"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u3AwQZTbtfc) when I first started studying and right before I took the test.
    It's a good overview of the topics on the test, but is nowhere near comprehensive.
- I watched the 12 videos in the ["FAA Part 107 Exam Study Guides"](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLRd2JSjVHovGabIuGeoupZgkzGmdys4Ol) playlist.
    He's pretty long winded and particular, but he covered most things on the test.
    His videos are long, so watch at at least 1.5x speed.
- Reading sectional charts is the part most people struggle with, so it's worth spending extra time there.
    A good chunk of the test comes back to pulling information off of a chart, to make sure you can read them. 

Other Resources:

- [This](https://free-faa-exam.kingschools.com/drone-pilot) is a practice exam that might be useful.
    I didn't use it, so I can't say if it is good or not.

Important things to note about the exam:

- It costs $175 every time you take it. You pay this to the testing center (PSI), not to the FAA.
- You are given 2 hours to take the test. If you've prepared, you shouldn't have much problem completing the test.
- There are 60 questions on the test, with the typical format being 3 options per question.
- You must get 70% of the questions right to pass. This is 42 questions.
- If you fail, you have to wait 14 calendar days before you can retake it, and you pay the $175 again.
    Another reason to cram hard and only schedule the test once you're ready.
- Your certificate itself never expires, but you have to stay current every 24 months to keep using it.
    See the Staying Current section below.
- The closest testing center is at the Provo airport through UVU, but there are other ones around.

## Registering for the Exam

1. Go to [psiexams](https://faa.psiexams.com/faa/login).
2. Sign in using the same login for your FAA account.
3. Search for and select "Unmanned Aircraft General - Small (UAG)". Confirm that you selected the correct test.
4. Follow the prompts to fill out the information for signing up for the test.
    (I can't reregister for the test again to fully outline the process, but it is straightforward)

### Exam Day

- Bring a valid government-issued photo ID. They won't let you test without one.
- Bring your FTN.
- Show up early. Checking in takes a few minutes and you don't want to be rushed before a timed test.
- The test is closed book, but the testing center hands you an official FAA supplement booklet with all of the charts and figures that the questions reference.
    You aren't expected to have the sectional charts memorized, just to be able to read one.
    The FAA supplement booklet can be found [here](https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/training_testing/testing/supplements/sport_rec_private_akts.pdf). 
    Useful for stuying sectional charts, since these are the ones the test will use. 

## After You Pass

### Applying for Your Certificate

Passing the exam does not give you your certificate.
You still have to apply for it. 

1. Wait for your test results to make it into IACRA. 
    This can take up to 48 hours after you test. 
    You can apply before this however. 
2. Log back into [IACRA](https://iacra.faa.gov/IACRA/SelectRoles.aspx) using the account you already made.
3. Click "Start New Application", then select Application Type "Pilot", Certifications "Remote Pilot", then "Start Application".
    This is FAA Form 8710-13.
4. Fill out the application. You'll need the knowledge test exam ID off of your test results.
5. Sign the application electronically and submit it.

Once it's submitted, the application goes to the TSA for a security background check.
When that clears you'll get an email telling you to log back into IACRA and print your temporary certificate.
The temporary certificate is good for 120 days and you can legally fly with it, so print it and keep a copy with you.
The permanent plastic card comes in the mail sometime inside those 120 days.

### Staying Current

To keep your certificate current, every 24 calendar months you have to complete a free online course to keep flying under Part 107.

- The course is "Part 107 Small UAS Recurrent" (ALC-677) on [FAASafety.gov](https://www.faasafety.gov/gslac/ALC/CourseLanding.aspx?cID=677).
- It's free and entirely online.
- Save the completion certificate when you finish, since that's your proof that you're current.

## Registering Drones

Your Part 107 covers you as the pilot.
The drone itself is a separate registration, and you need both before you can legally fly.
Verifiy the drones you are flying are registered. 

- Register each drone at [FAADroneZone](https://faadronezone-access.faa.gov/). It's $5 per aircraft and lasts 3 years.
- Register it under Part 107, not under the recreational rules.
    Registering under Part 107 requires that you already have your remote pilot certificate, so do this after the section above.
- **There is no 250g exemption under Part 107.** Recreational flyers can skip registration under 250g, but flying under Part 107 means every drone gets registered no matter how light it is.
- You'll get an N-number for each aircraft. Mark it somewhere visible on the outside of the drone. It can be on a sticker or drawn on. 
- Your drone also has to meet Remote ID requirements, which is a separate thing from registering it.
    Most drones sold recently broadcast Remote ID already, but older ones may need a broadcast module added on.
